title: Labor Department Freezes PERM Green-Card Filings for Microsoft, Adobe, Six IT Firms
excerpt: The October 8 suspension stops new and pending PERM labor certifications for eight employers under investigation. It does not cancel H-1B visas, and no fraud finding or written end date has been published.
body:
• The Labor Department said on October 8 it will not accept new or process pending PERM labor-certification applications for eight employers: Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini.
  • The freeze covers the PERM step only. It does not cancel existing H-1B visas, and reporting to date does not show it reaching PERM cases already certified or I-140 petitions already approved.
  • If you work for one of the eight and have a PERM case pending or planned, expect delay, not denial: check your sponsoring legal entity, your PERM stage and your H-1B expiry date, and confirm next steps with immigration counsel.
  • No written Labor Department notice, formal end date or finding of fraud against the eight companies has been published. The fraud claims are allegations under investigation, not proven violations.

The U.S. Department of Labor has suspended PERM labor-certification processing for Microsoft, Adobe and six large information technology services firms, halting a first step in most employer-sponsored green-card cases for workers at those companies while federal investigations proceed.

https://x.com/ChristinaNewstv/status/2112438677066350746

Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling announced the action on October 8 at a White House event alongside Vice President JD Vance. Sonderling said Microsoft and Adobe were suspended in connection with multiple active federal investigations, and he named Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini among the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world.

"We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies."

— Keith Sonderling, U.S. Secretary of Labor

PERM, the Permanent Labor Certification program, is administered by the Labor Department, not by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. Under the program described by the department's Office of Foreign Labor Certification, an employer must obtain a certified labor certification before filing an immigrant petition with USCIS for most EB-2 and EB-3 cases, certifying that no sufficient U.S. workers are able, willing, qualified and available for the job.

Vance focused his remarks on Microsoft. He said the company laid off 6,000 American workers last year while receiving 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards, and he accused the company of abusing the system more than any other U.S. employer. Sonderling said the eight companies together had requested almost 3 million foreign workers since 2009, received more than 230,000 H-1B approvals and obtained more than 100,000 permanent labor certifications.

Those figures are the administration's case, not a finding. The Washington Post reported that Vance did not present evidence that Microsoft had replaced laid-off American workers with foreign workers through the H-1B program. No charges or findings against the eight companies were announced.

Microsoft disputed the framing. It said about 80 percent of the roughly 6,000 H-1B applications it filed in the last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of existing employees, that the rest involved new hires already living legally in the United States and about 1 percent of its U.S. workforce, and that it pays H-1B employees the same as others in comparable work. Tata Consultancy Services said it did not expect a material impact on its workforce strategy.

The provision cited by immigration lawyers is 20 CFR 656.31(b), which allows the department to suspend PERM processing for an employer under investigation for possible fraud or willful misrepresentation until the investigation or proceedings end. Such a suspension may last initially for up to 180 days, after which the National Certifying Officer may resume processing or extend it. Debarment, a separate sanction of up to three years, has not been reported as applied to any of the eight.

For Indian professionals, who make up a large share of H-1B holders at the named firms, the effect depends on stage. A worker whose PERM is unfiled or pending with one of the eight cannot advance to an I-140 petition through that employer while the freeze holds. A worker with an approved I-140 is at a later stage the announcement, as reported, does not target. Current H-1B or OPT status is not cancelled, but workers approaching the six-year H-1B limit face added risk because extensions beyond six years often depend on a pending or approved labor certification or I-140.

Vance also said nine universities would be investigated over J-1 exchange-visitor visas. No end date was given, and Vance said the suspension would remain until the administration saw changes. What happens next turns on documents that have not yet appeared: as of the reporting reviewed here, the action had been announced at a press conference rather than in a Federal Register notice or a detailed written Labor Department order specifying the legal entities covered and the treatment of already-certified cases. Employers and workers are waiting for that guidance and for word on whether processing resumes, is extended, or expands.
